lessons.title: Negotiation Is Emotional, Not Rational
lessons.key_idea: People decide with their emotions first, so winning a negotiation starts with understanding feelings rather than out-arguing someone with logic.

lessons.title: Mirror Them and Slow Down
lessons.key_idea: Repeating the last few words someone said, in a calm and slow voice, makes them feel heard and gets them to reveal more.

lessons.title: Name Their Feelings Out Loud
lessons.key_idea: Labeling the other person's emotions, and even listing their likely complaints about you up front, defuses fear and builds trust.

lessons.title: Aim for No, Then That's Right
lessons.key_idea: Letting people say no makes them feel safe and in control, and hearing them say that's right signals they truly feel understood.

lessons.title: Ask How and What Questions
lessons.key_idea: Open questions that start with how or what give the other side the feeling of control while quietly steering them toward solving your problem.

lessons.title: Hunt for the Hidden Black Swans
lessons.key_idea: Every tool in the book serves one purpose: uncovering the surprising unknown facts that can transform a deal, instead of settling for splitting the difference.

plan.title: Never Split the Difference
plan.author: Chris Voss with Tahl Raz
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core techniques and structure well, including mirroring, labeling, calibrated questions and black swans, though I may not recall every anecdote in exact detail.
plan.one_liner: A former FBI hostage negotiator shows how listening, not logic, wins almost every negotiation.
plan.summary: Chris Voss spent years as the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator. In this book he argues that most negotiation advice gets people wrong. We are not calm, rational deal makers. We are emotional creatures who decide with our feelings first. So the best negotiators don't argue harder. They listen better. Voss calls this tactical empathy: understanding the other side's feelings and showing them you understand. He turns it into practical tools you can use anywhere, from salary talks to buying a car to getting your kids to bed. These tools include repeating someone's last words back to them, naming their emotions out loud, inviting them to say no, and asking open questions that start with how or what. The goal is never a lazy compromise. It is uncovering hidden information that changes everything.
